crime.value: Serial child abduction, torture, molestation, and murder across Midwest; central question: who is the vigilante who executed the killer and how was the perpetrator finally located?
crime.quote: They eventually found twelve others. Eleven of them were girls between the ages of five and eleven...All of them had been tortured and molested.

victim.value: Greg Day (alias Ringo Wink Pitchwinger), a prolific serial killer of children; 'killable' because he murdered at least 13 children across the Midwest over decades, making him a target for revenge justice.
victim.quote: "Greg Day?" he asked. Wink nodded yes and the man raised his gun and blew Wink's head off.

culprit_and_motive.value: Unknown vigilante (possibly rogue FBI agent, family member of victim, or bounty hunter) executes Greg Day/Wink; motive is revenge for murdered children or official justice.
culprit_and_motive.quote: I never did find out who the stranger was who had finished off Wink. Maybe it was a rogue FBI agent. Maybe it was the father or brother of one of the girls killed.

resolution.value: FBI investigation uncovers Greg Day's identity and locates remains of 13 victims across multiple Midwest graveyards; vigilante killer eliminates Day before formal prosecution; narrator becomes suspect but is eventually cleared.
resolution.quote: A day later a team from the FBI showed up...On that very same day, they found the remains of the first child.

investigator.value: First-person narrator (unnamed diner regular and bar patron); an unwitting accomplice who befriends the killer, becomes witness to execution, and is interrogated but ultimately exonerated.
investigator.quote: I had blood and bits of Wink all over me. At first the county sheriff thought I was involved somehow.

suspect_architecture.value: Single perpetrator (Wink/Greg Day) revealed posthumously; no competing suspects during narrative. Investigator-narrator briefly treated as suspect by county sheriff and community rumor.
suspect_architecture.quote: At first the county sheriff thought I was involved somehow. Or at least that's the way it seemed.

red_herring.value: Wink's eccentric, harmless persona — his silly jokes, bad clothes, drunken camaraderie, and apparent fondness for a tree stump — functions as sustained misdirection masking his identity as a serial child killer.
red_herring.quote: My life was neither richer nor poorer for having known him... I remembered he looked strange, but I couldn't remember his face.

clue_fairness.value: Clues are present but partially suppressed: Annie and Gifford both signal prior knowledge of Wink; the fake name yields no Google results; the stump visits are never explained. Reader has access to same data as narrator but significance is withheld until the FBI reveal.
clue_fairness.quote: I also think I've seen him before. I just can't figure out where... 'He's been around here before,' Gifford said.

social_world.value: Post-industrial dying town (Tivoli, Indiana) stripped of economic and institutional power after auto plant closure; residual community of elderly left-behinds with weak law enforcement, social insularity, and strong stigma dynamics that punish association with outsiders.
social_world.quote: People were polite to me, but there was a certain brittleness whenever they talked to me.

alibi.value: Wink claims he has never been in Indiana before, directly contradicting Annie's and Gifford's independent recollections; his alias 'Pitchwinger' produces zero records, undermining any verifiable identity or alibi structure.
alibi.quote: He said he'd never even been in the state of Indiana before... Your name doesn't exist. There's no such thing as a name Pitchwinger.

reveal_mechanic.value: Revelation delivered externally by a silent gunman who names the real identity (Greg Day), confirmed by Wink's own nod; followed by FBI discovery of thirteen children's remains on and near the stump site, retroactively decoding all prior behavior.
reveal_mechanic.quote: 'Greg Day?' he asked. 'How did you find me?' Wink asked... the man raised his gun and blew Wink's head off.

media_and_audience.value: No press coverage depicted within narrative; FBI arrives and departs with minimal engagement; community processes the crime through gossip, whisper, and social ostracism of the narrator rather than formal public discourse.
media_and_audience.quote: I heard the whispers and the gossip and the innuendos... Most people thought that somehow I was involved in the last child's death.

investigator_wound.value: Narrator's defining trait is inability to imagine alternatives or act on instinct ('What-ifs made me feel uncomfortable'); this same incuriosity causes him to ignore every warning sign about Wink, making his psychological rigidity the direct enabler of his complicity.
investigator_wound.quote: That was pretty much my problem, I guess. I wasn't one for imagining things. What-ifs made me feel uncomfortable.

_meta.title: The Man Who Fell in Love with the Stump
_meta.author: RANDY RO H N
